title: Shopping at the Souq
description: Ask the price, hear the answer in riyals or dinars, count from eleven to a hundred, say it's too expensive and ask for a discount — the bargaining script of a traditional Gulf souq, and when not to use it.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — transactional script. Market walk-throughs supply the prices; the learner drills the numbers with counted nouns, then runs the whole buying exchange aloud from opening price to change.
unlock_condition: ≥13/17 on the price-and-number listening quiz and a complete recorded purchase (ask, react, offer, pay)
can_do: Buy something and ask the price
Count from eleven to a hundred with the noun in the right form
Say expensive, cheap and ask for a discount

grammar.title: Numbers with things: 3–10 take a plural, 11 and up take a singular
grammar.explanation: One and two need no number word — you say the noun alone (ريال) or its dual form with ـين (ريالين 'two riyals'). From three to ten the number comes first in its short form and the thing goes plural: ثلاث ريالات، خمس دنانير، عشر دقايق. From eleven upwards the thing snaps back to the singular: خمسطعش ريال، عشرين درهم، مية ريال. The teens all end in ـطعش (khamsṭaʿash, siṭṭaʿash) and the tens in ـين (ʿishriin, thalaathiin). Compounds put the unit first: واحد وعشرين 'one and twenty'. Gulf speakers are relaxed about the masculine/feminine number forms formal Arabic drills, so do not worry about them — the short form before any plural is normal.

grammar.title: بكم؟ — how much is this, how much for the kilo
grammar.explanation: The price question is بكم (bikam), 'with how much', and the answer comes back with the same بـ: بكم هذا؟ — بعشرين ريال. To ask for the price of a quantity, name the quantity after it: بكم الكيلو؟ 'how much is the kilo?'. For the total, كم الكل؟ or كم الحساب؟. Kuwaitis say بچم with their soft ك. Two follow-ups every buyer needs: آخر سعر؟ 'last price?' and فيه خصم؟ 'is there a discount?'. The formal بكم هذا الشيء or كم ثمنه would sound like a phrasebook.

examples.english: How much is this? — Twenty riyals

culture.title: The bargaining script — and where it does not apply
culture.note: In a traditional souq the first price is an opening, not an insult. Ask بكم؟, react with a soft غالي 'expensive', ask آخر سعر؟, and offer something in between; the seller will come down a step, you go up a step, and a smile and يعطيك العافية close it. Walking away slowly is part of the dance and often brings the real price. But bargaining has borders: never in a mall, a supermarket, a chain café, a pharmacy or anywhere the price is printed — there it is simply rude. Gold is priced by weight each day, so you bargain only on the making charge. On leaving any shop, bought or not, يعطيك العافية to the seller.

phrases.english: Expensive! Bring it down a bit
Thanks for your work (said on leaving)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The everyday 'buy'; the past is شريت (shirayt) — the short Gulf form of اشتريت, which you will meet in the past-tense lesson. Never the formal أبتاع.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand handing banknotes across a market counter and receiving a bag of fruit.

example.arabic: أشتري خضار من السوق كل جمعة
example.transliteration: ashtiri khuḍaar min is-suug kill jumʿa
example.english: I buy vegetables from the market every Friday

vocabulary.video_hint: A grocery-haul vlog: أشتري / شريت said as items are shown.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Hollow verb: أبيع، يبيع، باع. The seller is البياع. Ends in ع — hold the throat sound.
vocabulary.image_scene: A stallholder behind a table of dates and spices, holding up a bag toward the camera.

example.english: He sells dates at the market

vocabulary.video_hint: A seller describing what they sell; a sign saying للبيع.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Soft gargled غ at the start. The bargaining word — said with a small wince. Also the affectionate يا الغالي 'my dear' (literally 'precious one'), so tone is everything. Feminine غالية.
vocabulary.image_scene: A price tag with a large number on it, a shopper's eyebrows raised.
vocabulary.video_hint: A shopper reacting to a price — غالي! — in a market or challenge video.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The opposite of غالي; long ii, emphatic ص. The verb رخّص 'make it cheaper' is what you ask the seller to do. Feminine رخيصة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small price tag with a tiny number and a shopper giving a thumbs-up.
vocabulary.video_hint: A 'cheapest vs most expensive' challenge; رخيص said over a low price.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables in Gulf: khaṣim. فيه خصم؟ 'is there a discount?' works in souq and mall alike; the sale season is التخفيضات or the English سيل.
vocabulary.image_scene: A red sign reading 50% hanging over a rack of clothes.

example.english: Is there a discount on this?

vocabulary.video_hint: A shopper asking فيه خصم؟ or a vlog about التخفيضات with sale signs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Borrowed, so free. Fruit, vegetables, meat and dates are all sold by the kilo; بكم الكيلو؟ is the market question. Half a kilo is نص كيلو.
vocabulary.image_scene: A market scale with a pile of tomatoes on it, the needle at 1 kg.

example.english: Give me a kilo of tomatoes

vocabulary.video_hint: Produce being weighed at a stall; الكيلو in the price exchange.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The plastic or paper bag the seller puts things in; long ii. A handbag or shopping bag you carry is a شنطة — you will hear both at a checkout: تبي كيس؟ 'do you want a bag?'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A plastic shopping bag full of fruit being handed over a counter.

example.english: Do you want a bag? — Yes, please

vocabulary.video_hint: A checkout or stall where goods go into a bag; كيس or شنطة said.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two syllables: si-ʿir, with ع in the middle. آخر سعر 'last price' is the bargaining phrase; the formal ثمن is not used.
vocabulary.image_scene: A handwritten price card propped against a bowl of dates.

example.english: The price is high — last price?

vocabulary.video_hint: Prices being compared or negotiated — السعر — in a market video.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The small neighbourhood shop; a corner grocery is a بقالة, a mall store is a محل. Doubled k, long aa. Plural دكاكين.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small corner shop with a striped awning, crates of fruit outside, a man in a thobe at the door.

example.english: The shop is next to the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: A corner shop or بقالة visited in a vlog; the word said at the door.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first of the tens, all ending in ـين: ثلاثين، أربعين، خمسين… ستين، سبعين، ثمانين، تسعين. After a ten the noun stays singular: عشرين ريال. Twenty-one is واحد وعشرين — unit first.
vocabulary.image_scene: A twenty-riyal-style banknote with the number 20 large and clear.
vocabulary.video_hint: A price with عشرين / ثلاثين / خمسين said as money changes hands.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said miya, not the formal miʾa; before a noun it grows a t: مية ريال is miyat riyaal. Two hundred is ميتين, then ثلاث مية and so on; a thousand is ألف.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hundred-riyal-style banknote with the number 100 large and clear.

example.english: All together it's a hundred riyals

vocabulary.video_hint: A budget challenge — تحدي بمية ريال — or a total of مية said aloud.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The formal نصف loses its f: nuṣṣ, doubled emphatic ص. نص كيلو half a kilo; نص ساعة half an hour; it returns in telling time.
vocabulary.image_scene: A watermelon cut cleanly in half on a market table.

example.english: I want half a kilo of dates

vocabulary.video_hint: A quantity ordered — نص كيلو — at a stall.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'The remainder', with ق as g: il-baagi. When you hand over a big note the seller asks ما عندك فراطة؟ 'no small change?'; when you want yours back, وين الباقي؟. Keep the ال on it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A cashier's hand returning coins and a small note into a customer's palm.
vocabulary.video_hint: Paying at a till; الباقي handed back or waved away.

vocabulary.english: I need / I'm in need of
vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf speakers say 'I need' with this participle more than with a verb: محتاج كيس 'I need a bag', feminine محتاجة. It is softer than لازم and the shop form of asking for something. Kuwaitis also say يبيلي 'it wants for me'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopper holding an empty basket looking at a shelf with a thoughtful face.
vocabulary.video_hint: A shopper telling a seller what they need — محتاج / أحتاج — before buying.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf says kithiir with a th (not the Egyptian kitiir). Said alone about a price it means 'that's too much'. For 'very' the Gulf prefers واجد / وايد, coming in the weather lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A pile of banknotes far larger than the small item beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: A buyer objecting to a price — كثير! — and the seller coming down.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The phrase that skips to the end of the negotiation. Say it with a smile and the seller names the real price; anything below that means walking away.
vocabulary.image_scene: A buyer and a seller across a stall, the seller writing a number on a notepad.
vocabulary.video_hint: A haggling exchange where آخر سعر؟ is asked and answered.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The command form of 'make cheaper', from رخيص. Always softened with شوي 'a bit' or الله يخليك: رخّص شوي. Doubled kh in the middle.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand gesturing 'a little lower' over a price tag, the seller smiling.

example.english: Bring it down a bit, please

vocabulary.video_hint: A customer asking رخص شوي in a souq scene.

sound_spotlight.explanation: Eleven to nineteen all end in -ṭaʿash, a crushed form of عشر with an emphatic ṭ. The number word before it is chopped short, so fifteen is khams-ṭaʿash, not khamsa-ʿashar.

sound_spotlight.sound: بـ on both sides of the price
sound_spotlight.explanation: The same little b- opens the question and the answer. Hear it as 'for': for how much? — for twenty. It is not the future بـ.
Gulf keeps the th sound that Cairo turns into t or s. Thirty and eighty both start with it; put your tongue between your teeth.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second souq walk-through with prices audible and the numbers appearing on screen as digits — the learner links the sound of عشرين to the figure 20 before any explanation.
Seventeen cards with illustration and audio; the numbers play inside a price (بعشرين ريال) so the singular noun after them is heard from the start.
Grammar card: ريالين / ثلاث ريالات / خمسطعش ريال built with audio; then a drag exercise pairing numbers with the right noun form for ريال، دينار، كيلو، دقيقة.
Listening quiz: fifteen prices spoken at market speed; the learner types the digits. Wrong answers replay the number slowly with its ـطعش or ـين ending highlighted.
Role-play: the app plays a seller opening high; the learner asks بكم، reacts with غالي, asks آخر سعر, offers, and pays. Branching on what the learner offers.
Score screen; the learner's recorded purchase plays back next to a native one. Nudge: read every price you see today in Gulf.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Read the next three prices you see out loud in Gulf, with the noun: خمسطعش ريال، عشرين درهم، مية دينار.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Drills the 11+ singular rule on real numbers.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you buy anything from a person rather than a machine, open with بكم هذا؟ and close with يعطيك العافية — even if you don't bargain.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day nudge. The two phrases that bracket every Gulf purchase.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Watch a Saudi or Kuwaiti budget challenge — تحدي بمية ريال — and write down every price you hear.
real_world_prompts.context: Homework card. Number recognition at natural speed with the items on screen.
